title: Homeomorphisms
objectives: Prove two spaces are homeomorphic, or find a property that tells them apart.

screens.title: Squashing a square into a disc
screens.prose: Drag $P$ round the square $[-1, 1]^2$. Its image is $P' = P \cdot \tfrac{d_\infty(0, P)}{d_2(0, P)}$: the same direction, with $d_2(0, P') = d_\infty(0, P)$. Watch $P'$ trace the disc.
screens.question: Drag $P$ to the corner $(1, 1)$. What is the first coordinate of $P'$? Give four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Right. The corner lands on the circle at $45°$.

byKey.corner: 1 is $P$'s own coordinate. The map pulls the corner in to the circle.
byKey.half: You divided by 2 instead of by $d_2 = \sqrt2$.

explain.text: $d_\infty(0, (1, 1)) = 1$ and $d_2 = \sqrt2$, so $P' = (0.7071, 0.7071)$, on the unit circle. The square's rim goes onto the circle, ray by ray.

screens.title: Two more images
screens.prose: The map is a bijection from the square onto the disc. Its inverse multiplies by $\tfrac{d_2}{d_\infty}$ instead. Both are continuous away from 0 by their formulas. At 0 they are too, since $d_2(0, P') = d_\infty(0, P)$ and $d_\infty \le d_2 \le \sqrt2\, d_\infty$. Such a map is a **homeomorphism**, and we write $X \cong Y$.
screens.question: Fill in the images to four decimal places.

hints.text: Divide by $\sqrt{1.25} \approx 1.1180$; the second point is half the first.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each coordinate by $\tfrac{d_\infty}{d_2}$.

explain.text: $(1, 0.5)$ has $\tfrac{d_\infty}{d_2} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{1.25}}$, giving $(0.8944, 0.4472)$. The map keeps rays and scales lengths, so $(0.5, 0.25)$ goes to $(0.4472, 0.2236)$.

screens.title: An interval as big as the line
screens.question: Which map is the inverse $g : \mathbb{R} \to (-1, 1)$?

options.why: You dropped the absolute value. At $y = -9$ this gives $\tfrac{-9}{-8} > 1$, outside $(-1, 1)$.
You copied $f$. At $y = 3$ it gives $-1.5$, not 0.75.

hints.text: $x = \tfrac{y}{1 + y}$ for $y \ge 0$; the sign rule makes it $\tfrac{y}{1 + |y|}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each candidate at $y = 3$ and $y = -9$.

explain.text: For $y \ge 0$, $y(1 - x) = x$ gives $x = \tfrac{y}{1 + y}$; odd symmetry handles $y < 0$. So $g(y) = \tfrac{y}{1 + |y|}$, and $g(3) = 0.75$.

screens.title: The inverse on the left
screens.prose: For $y \ge 0$, $\tfrac{y}{1 + |y|}$ and $\tfrac{y}{1 + y}$ agree. A negative input tells them apart.
screens.question: What is $g(-3)$?

byKey.sign: You lost the sign. $g$ is odd: $g(-3) = -g(3)$.

explain.text: $g(-3) = \tfrac{-3}{1 + 3} = -0.75$. Without the absolute value we would get 1.5, which is not even in $(-1, 1)$.

screens.title: Proving $(-1, 1) \cong \mathbb{R}$
screens.prose: We prove $f(x) = \tfrac{x}{1 - |x|}$ is a homeomorphism. Two middle lines may come in either order. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: $f$ is continuous on $(-1, 1)$: a quotient of continuous maps whose denominator $1 - |x|$ is positive.
$g(f(x)) = x$ for $x \in (-1, 1)$ and $f(g(y)) = y$ for $y \in \mathbb{R}$, by direct substitution.
So $f$ is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse $g$: $(-1, 1) \cong \mathbb{R}$. $\blacksquare$
$f$ is a continuous bijection, so it is a homeomorphism.
lines.why: A continuous bijection need not have a continuous inverse. The inverse needs its own proof.

hints.text: Three things: $f$ continuous, $g$ continuous, and they undo each other.
Continuity of $f$ and $g$ first, then the identities, then the conclusion.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Prove each map continuous, then that they are inverse.

byKey.d1: You skipped the inverse. Continuity of a bijection does not make its inverse continuous.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Both $f$ and $g$ are quotients with denominators that never vanish, so both are continuous. Substitution shows they undo each other. So $f$ is a homeomorphism.

screens.title: Telling spaces apart
screens.prose: A homeomorphism keeps every property defined by open sets. Removing a point is one test: a homeomorphism $h$ restricts to one between $X \setminus \{x\}$ and $Y \setminus \{h(x)\}$.
screens.question: Prove $[0, 1) \not\cong (0, 1)$. Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Then $h$ restricts to a homeomorphism from $(0, 1)$ onto $(0, 1) \setminus \{h(0)\}$.
$(0, 1)$ is one piece, while removing any point from $(0, 1)$ leaves two pieces.
A homeomorphism keeps the number of pieces, so this is impossible. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Remove 0 from $[0, 1)$ and its image from $(0, 1)$.

feedback.correct: Right. The end point gives it away.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Assume $h$ exists, remove 0, and count pieces.

explain.text: Removing 0 from $[0, 1)$ leaves the single piece $(0, 1)$. Removing any point from $(0, 1)$ leaves two. Homeomorphisms keep pieces, which l8 calls components, so no $h$ exists.

screens.title: Letters
screens.prose: The letters T, X and Y are drawn as unions of segments. Remove the junction point of each letter.
screens.question: Removing the junction of X leaves how many pieces?

hints.text: Count the arms meeting at the junction.
T and Y give 3, X gives 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the arms of X.

byKey.three: 3 is the count for T and Y. X has four arms.
byKey.two: You counted the two strokes. Cutting their crossing makes four arms.

explain.text: T and Y each leave 3 pieces, X leaves 4. A homeomorphism T to X would send the junction somewhere, and no point of X leaves 3 pieces. So T $\not\cong$ X, while bending Y's arms shows T $\cong$ Y.

screens.title: Finite spaces up to relabelling
screens.prose: Between finite spaces a homeomorphism is a relabelling of points carrying $\tau$ onto $\tau'$. On $\{a, b\}$, swapping $a$ and $b$ carries $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, X\}$ onto $\{\varnothing, \{b\}, X\}$.
screens.question: How many homeomorphism classes do the four topologies on two points form?

hints.text: Which two rows does a swap match?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Merge the rows a relabelling matches.

byKey.four: You counted the two Sierpiński spaces separately. A swap of labels makes them the same space.
byKey.two: Discrete and indiscrete differ: one has 4 open sets, the other 2.

explain.text: A relabelling keeps the number of open sets, so the classes have 2, 3 and 4 open sets. On three points the 29 topologies fall into 9 classes. Sierpiński and discrete are not homeomorphic.

screens.title: A continuous bijection that is not enough
screens.prose: The map $h(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$ from $[0, 2\pi)$ onto the unit circle is continuous and one-to-one onto. The points $t_n = 2\pi - \tfrac1n$ are marked on the circle.
screens.question: Is $h$ a homeomorphism?

options.text: No: $h(t_n) \to (1, 0) = h(0)$, but $t_n \to 2\pi$, far from 0, so $h^{-1}$ jumps at $(1, 0)$.
Yes: it is continuous and a bijection.
options.why: You took a continuous bijection to be a homeomorphism. The inverse must be continuous too, and it tears the circle at $(1, 0)$.

options.text: No: it is not one-to-one, since $h(0) = h(2\pi)$.
options.why: $2\pi$ is not in $[0, 2\pi)$, so $h$ is one-to-one.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Test the inverse along $h(t_n)$.

byKey.yes: You stopped at continuity of $h$. Its inverse sends points just below $(1, 0)$ to near $2\pi$, a jump.

explain.text: Images of $t_n$ approach $(1, 0) = h(0)$, yet $t_n$ approaches $2\pi$, not 0. So $h^{-1}$ is not continuous at $(1, 0)$. Level 3 shows compactness of the domain would have saved it.

screens.title: Homeomorphisms by machine
screens.prose: A map between finite spaces is a dict. Write `is_continuous(f, tau_X, tau_Y)`: every preimage of an open set is open. Then write `are_homeomorphic(X, tau_X, Y, tau_Y)`, trying every bijection. Hidden helpers `T(...)` and `norm(...)` are available. Checking cases is evidence, not proof.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from itertools import permutations

def is_continuous(f, tau_X, tau_Y):
    """True if every preimage under the dict f of a set in tau_Y is in tau_X."""
    ...

def are_homeomorphic(X, tau_X, Y, tau_Y):
    """True if some bijection X -> Y carries tau_X onto tau_Y."""
    ...
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, compared exactly. Five test is_continuous (identities between discrete and indiscrete, a swap, a constant map). Five test are_homeomorphic: the two Sierpiński spaces, Sierpiński against discrete, two chains, a chain against $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$, and different sizes. The first Check starts Python in the browser, about 4 s once.

hints.text: A preimage is `frozenset(x for x in f if f[x] in V)`.
For each permutation, compare the image of `tau_X` with `tau_Y` as sets.

feedback.correct: Right. Relabelling decides homeomorphism on finite spaces.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check every preimage, and every bijection.

explain.text: A bijection carrying $\tau_X$ onto $\tau_Y$ is continuous both ways, so it is a homeomorphism. The chain $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ is no relabelling of $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$, which is not a chain.

screens.title: Fitting a correlation freely
screens.prose: A calibrator fits a correlation $\rho \in (-1, 1)$ by optimising $z = \operatorname{artanh}\rho$ over all of $\mathbb{R}$, then maps back with $\rho = \tanh z$. Since $\tanh$ is a homeomorphism, close in $z$ means close in $\rho$. The optimiser never leaves the valid range.
screens.question: Fill in the table to four decimal places.

feedback.correct: Right. The whole of $\mathbb{R}$ maps onto $(-1, 1)$.

byKey.same: You took $z = \rho$. That holds only near 0; $\operatorname{artanh} 0.5 = \tfrac12\ln 3$.

explain.text: $z = \tfrac12\ln 3 \approx 0.5493$ and $\tfrac12\ln\tfrac{0.1}{1.9} \approx -1.4722$, while $\tanh 1 \approx 0.7616$. A volatility is fitted the same way as $\ln\sigma$. The closed range $[-1, 1]$ cannot be treated so: it is compact and $\mathbb{R}$ is not, as level 3 shows.

ideas: A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. The square is homeomorphic to the disc, and $(-1, 1)$ to $\mathbb{R}$ via $\tfrac{x}{1 - |x|}$.

Properties defined by open sets survive homeomorphisms. Removing a point and counting pieces tells $[0, 1)$ from $(0, 1)$, and T from X. Finite spaces match by relabelling: 3 classes on two points, 9 on three.
A continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism: $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ on $[0, 2\pi)$ has a discontinuous inverse. Boundedness is not kept: $(-1, 1) \cong \mathbb{R}$.

formula.name: Homeomorphism
formula.tex: h : X \to Y \text{ bijective}, \quad h \text{ and } h^{-1} \text{ continuous}

summary.trap: A continuous bijection is not automatically a homeomorphism: $[0, 2\pi)$ onto the circle tears at $(1, 0)$.

quiz.question: What does this say about boundedness?

options.text: It is not a topological property: a bounded space is homeomorphic to an unbounded one
Homeomorphisms keep boundedness, so $\mathbb{R}$ is bounded
options.why: $\mathbb{R}$ is unbounded in its usual metric. Boundedness depends on the metric, not the open sets.
We proved $f$ is one. The conclusion is that boundedness is not kept.

feedback.correct: Right. Boundedness belongs to the metric.
feedback.generic: Not quite. One space is bounded, the other not, yet they are homeomorphic.

explain.text: $(-1, 1)$ is bounded, $\mathbb{R}$ is not, and they are homeomorphic. So boundedness is not determined by the open sets. Level 3 finds the same for completeness.

quiz.prose: Let $\mathrm{id}$ map $\{a, b\}$ with the discrete topology to $\{a, b\}$ with the indiscrete topology.
quiz.question: Is $\mathrm{id}$ a homeomorphism?

options.text: No: it is a continuous bijection, but its inverse is not continuous
Yes: the identity is always a homeomorphism
options.why: You trusted the continuous bijection. The inverse pulls the open $\{a\}$ back to $\{a\}$, which is not open in the indiscrete space.
Out of a discrete space every map is continuous. The inverse is the problem.

feedback.correct: Right. The same trap as the circle.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test $\mathrm{id}$ and its inverse separately.

explain.text: $\mathrm{id}$ is continuous, since every set is open in the discrete domain. Its inverse needs $\{a\}$ open in the indiscrete space, and it is not.

quiz.prose: There are 29 topologies on three points.
quiz.question: How many homeomorphism classes do they form?

widget.accept: 9, by trying all six relabellings of each topology.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Merge topologies that a relabelling matches.

byKey.all: 29 counts topologies, not classes. Relabellings merge many of them.
byKey.six: 6 is the number of relabellings of three points, not of classes.

explain.text: Grouping the 29 topologies by the six relabellings of $\{a, b, c\}$ leaves 9 classes. On 0 to 3 points the class counts are 1, 1, 3 and 9.
